newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.African judges vie for top court position.
newsitem.headline: S.African judges vie for top court position.

text.p: The parallel streams of black and white experience in apartheid's courts came to the fore on Friday when South Africa's Judicial Service Commission publicly interviewed rival candidates for the post of Chief Justice.

On the basis of the country's first public interviews of judicial candidates, the statutory commission will advise President Nelson Mandela on a choice between a flamboyant ethnic Indian and a dour white Afrikaner.

Constitutional Court Judge Ismail Mahomed, 65, who told the panel he was able to overcome the humiliations and handicaps of apartheid because "there was a moral passion within me to achieve justice"; and
Veteran Appeal Court Judge Hennie van Heerden, 65, who has spent most of his career in the conservative central Free State province, where little of his work involved apartheid cases.
"Apart from the law of unfair competition, I would say contract law was my first love," van Heerden said.

The race for the South African judiciary's top job turned sour recently when 100 of the country's 180 judges signed a petition in support of van Heerden and one of them asked Mahomed to "do the decent thing" and withdraw.

Most of the country's few black judges supported Mahomed and Mandela triggered a storm when he supported Mahomed's nomination in writing but said through a spokesman that this would not affect his final decision.
The candidates represent the opposite poles of opinion on how South Africa should reform a judiciary tainted by 45 years of often harsh enforcement of legislated racial segregation.
Mahomed said it was necessary to accelerate the training of black and female judges to ensure that the largely white, male courts better reflect the country's black-dominated society.

Van Heerden said he believed there was little that could be done quickly to challenge the public perception, which he believed was unfounded, that the courts had been servants of the apartheid government.
Black judges should be appointed as they became available, he said, "but not at the cost of standards".
The current Chief Justice, Michael Corbett, retires at the end of the year.
